subject: Anthropology
title: Language Death
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Language Death.

hook.text: A language dies every two weeks. When the last speaker falls silent, an entire worldview vanishes forever.

buildup.text: Language death occurs when a community stops transmitting its language to the next generation.

discovery.text: Of roughly 7,000 languages today, nearly half are endangered. Most have fewer than 10,000 speakers.

twist.text: Languages don't die naturally — they're killed by colonialism, economic pressure, and policies that punish speakers.

climax.text: Each lost language erases unique knowledge about plants, weather, history, and ways of understanding the world.

punchline.text: A lost language is a lost way of seeing.

quiz.question: What primarily causes language death?
options: Colonialism, economic pressure, and suppressive policies

details.summary: Language death occurs when the last fluent speakers of a language die without passing it to younger generations. Roughly half of the world's 7,000-plus languages are expected to disappear by 2100, taking unique cultural knowledge with them.
details.whyItMatters: Each language encodes unique knowledge about ecology, medicine, history, and philosophy. Language death represents irreversible loss of human intellectual heritage, comparable to losing biological species.
takeaways: Roughly half of all languages may vanish by the end of the century
Languages die when transmission to children ceases
Each lost language takes unique cultural knowledge with it

faq.question: What causes languages to die?
faq.answer: Dominant languages spread through education, media, economic opportunity, and government policy. Parents may choose to raise children in the dominant language for practical advantages. Forced assimilation, as in colonial boarding schools, accelerates language death dramatically.

faq.question: Can dead languages be revived?
faq.answer: Hebrew was successfully revived as a daily spoken language after centuries of primarily liturgical use. Other revitalization efforts, including Welsh and Hawaiian, have achieved significant success. Complete revival from extinction is extremely rare but partial recovery is achievable.
